jsnvu6-e178597-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 1: whether we need habits, with a reference to Aquinas's parallel treatment.

jsnvu6-e178597-d1e115.summary: Lays out the plan of the distinction—habits in general, faith in particular, then the formation and unformedness of faith—and opens the first question with an argument that we do not need habits: humans are intermediate between angels and brutes, and brutes have no habits.
claims: The questions on d.23 treat habits in general, faith in particular, and formed vs. unformed faith
Since brutes have no habits, neither do humans, who share in animal nature (objection)
concepts: human as intermediate between angels and brutes

jsnvu6-e178597-d1e133.summary: Second argument against habits: by Ethics II, acts preceding the habit are like those following it except in facility; but facility diminishes merit, since difficulty increases it; so the habit does more harm than good. It anticipates the common reply that difficulty from the work increases merit while difficulty from the agent diminishes it, and the habit removes only the latter.
claims: Acts before and after a habit differ only in facility (Aristotle)
If habits only produce facility, they diminish merit (objection)

jsnvu6-e178597-d1e167.summary: Rejoinders reinforcing the objection: the widow's two mites (Mark 12, Luke 21) show that difficulty arising from the agent's condition—her poverty—increases merit, undercutting the common reply; and since rational powers are more perfect than natural powers, which need no habits either for their act or for its manner, rational powers do not need them either.
claims: Difficulty from the condition of the agent can increase merit (objection)
Natural powers need no habits, so neither do the more perfect rational powers (objection)

jsnvu6-e178597-d1e189.summary: Argument for the opposite from Aristotle's Ethics II: the soul contains power, habit, and act; since we need the extremes—powers and acts—we need the middle, habits.
claims: We need habits because they mediate between powers and acts

jsnvu6-e178597-d1e202.summary: Second argument for the opposite: by Metaphysics V a habit is that by which one is well or ill disposed in itself or toward another; we need what disposes us well, so at least good habits are needed.
claims: At least good habits are needed, since they dispose us well

jsnvu6-e178597-d1e213.summary: Outline of the response: first, determine the senses in which 'habit' is said; from this the answer to whether we need habits will follow.

jsnvu6-e178597-d1e224.summary: Begins the first article by distinguishing three senses of 'habit': as a postpraedicamentum, as a category, and as a determinate species of quality; the name derives from 'having' (habere), which yields two derivations.
claims: 'Habit' is said in three ways: postpredicament, category, and species of quality

jsnvu6-e178597-d1e242.summary: Explains the two derivations from 'having': (1) one thing having another, and (2) a thing being disposed somehow. Under the first, all ways of having reduce to three: having an inherent accident (which spans categories and is thus a postpredicament), having a correlative (reducible to relation), and having by way of ornament, such as clothing or arms, which constitutes the special category of habitus.
claims: Ways of 'having' reduce to inherence, correlation, and adornment
Habitus as category is having by way of ornament, as being clothed or armed

jsnvu6-e178597-d1e287.summary: The second derivation—a thing being well or ill disposed in itself or toward another—gives habit as a species of quality, which, unlike the other senses, names the thing had rather than the relation of haver to had. This is the sense at issue. Two definitions are given: Aristotle's (Metaphysics V; Ethics II: power is that by which we can, habit that by which we can well or ill) and Averroes's (De anima III: a habit is that which one can use when one wills), echoed by Augustine in De bono coniugali.
claims: Habit as quality names the disposition itself, not a relation of possession
A habit is that by which we are disposed well or ill (Aristotle)
A habit is that which one can use when one wills (Averroes, Augustine)

jsnvu6-e178597-d1e339.summary: Determination: we have habits and need good ones, and bad ones are possible. From the first definition: powers indifferent to good and bad acts—intellect to truth and falsity, will and sensitive appetite to good and evil—need something determining them to the good, which is a good habit; and since good habits are not natural, their contraries are possible. From the second definition: powers that can suffer difficulty in acting, as the continent person against passion, need something facilitating action, which is a habit.
claims: We need good habits to determine indifferent powers to good acts
Bad habits are possible because good habits are not in us by nature
Powers that can suffer difficulty need habits to facilitate their acts

jsnvu6-e178597-d1e396.summary: Reply to the first argument: the intermediate shares some features with each extreme but not all. Humans share sensitive soul with brutes and intellect with angels, but it is proper to purely intellectual nature not to need habits unless joined to sense; so angels have no acquired habits. Brutes do have a kind of acquired habit through memory and custom (Aristotle, De memoria; Augustine on tamed beasts), but lack the full notion of habit since they lack dominion over its use; humans possess the full notion.
claims: Angels have no acquired habits, since pure intellectual nature does not need them
Brutes have customary habits but not habits in the full sense, lacking control over their use
Humans have habits in the full sense

jsnvu6-e178597-d1e455.summary: Reply to the second argument: we need habits for facility and determination to a certain mode. Facility from the agent, produced by habit, does not diminish but increases merit, other things being equal, because it increases voluntariness; only facility of the work diminishes merit. The widow's difficulty came from the work, not the agent, since poverty is a condition of fortune, not of the person: she gave more relative to what remained to her.
claims: Facility from habit increases merit by increasing voluntariness
Difficulty of the work, not of the agent, increases merit
The widow's greater merit stems from the proportion of gift to remaining goods

jsnvu6-e178597-d1e494.summary: Reply to the third argument: natural powers need no habits since they are determined to a single mode; rational powers are indeterminate and need determining habits, which shows not their imperfection but their greater perfection, since this indifference is rooted in their freedom and universality.
claims: Rational powers need habits because of their indeterminacy, which stems from their freedom and universality
Needing habits does not make rational powers less perfect than natural ones

jsnvu6-e178597.summary: Question 1 asks whether we need habits, opening Durandus's treatment of d.23 (habits in general, faith in particular, formed and unformed faith). Against habits: humans stand between angels and brutes, which lack habits; habit brings only facility, which seems to reduce merit (the widow's mite is pressed against the usual reply); natural powers need no habits. For habits: Aristotle's triad of power, habit, and act, and habit as what disposes us well. Durandus first distinguishes three senses of habitus—a postpredicament (having an inherent accident), the category of 'having' by way of adornment, and the species of quality by which a thing is well or ill disposed—and adopts the last, defined both by Aristotle (well or ill disposed) and by Averroes and Augustine (what one can use at will). He concludes that we need good habits and that bad ones are possible: indeterminate powers (intellect, will, sensitive appetite) need determination to the good, and powers subject to difficulty need facilitation. In the replies, angels lack acquired habits and brutes have only customary quasi-habits without control over their use; facility from the agent increases merit by increasing voluntariness; and the indeterminacy of rational powers that requires habits reflects their freedom and superiority.
claims: Habit in the relevant sense is a quality disposing a power well or ill and usable at will
Humans need good habits to determine and facilitate indeterminate rational and appetitive powers
Bad habits are possible since good habits are not natural
Facility arising from habit increases rather than diminishes merit
Angels have no acquired habits; brutes have only customary habits lacking the full notion
